title: Systematic Theology I: Scripture, God and the Trinity
description: The first of three courses in systematic theology. Students study prolegomena (the nature and method of theology), the doctrine of revelation and Scripture, the existence and knowability of God, the divine attributes, the doctrine of the Trinity, and God's decrees, creation and providence. The course reads the great theologians of every tradition - Athanasius, the Cappadocians, Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, Luther, Calvin, Wesley, Arminius and Hodge - and presents disputed questions (such as divine sovereignty and human freedom) fairly.

quiz_bank.question: How does systematic theology relate to biblical and historical theology?
quiz_bank.answer_key: Biblical theology studies Scripture's teaching in its historical development; historical theology studies how the church understood doctrine; systematic theology draws on both to present a coherent, topically organized account of what the whole Bible teaches for today.

quiz_bank.question: Compare the scholastic and inductive methods.
quiz_bank.answer_key: The scholastic method (Aquinas) proceeds by questions, objections, authorities and reasoned responses, using philosophy; the inductive method (Hodge) gathers and arranges the 'facts' of Scripture to derive doctrines. Both aim at faithful, orderly understanding of revealed truth.
